miniTms.description: Multi-tenant transportation management system with real-time delivery tracking — NestJS, Next.js, PostgreSQL and Redis pub/sub, built to demonstrate real domain modeling and a horizontally-scalable real-time architecture.

detail.overview: A multi-tenant transportation management system covering seller onboarding, carrier management, and real-time delivery tracking — built as a technical artifact, not a commercial product, to demonstrate real domain modeling and a horizontally-scalable real-time architecture.
architecture: Multi-layer RBAC across four roles — admin, seller, carrier, and operator — each with its own onboarding, approval, and permission boundaries.
Shipment assignment runs through a real coverage-and-modality matching engine, not a naive first-come queue.
Real-time tracking over Socket.io with a Redis adapter, so the WebSocket layer scales across multiple API instances instead of being pinned to one process.
stack: NestJS + Prisma (PostgreSQL) for a structured, testable backend with a real migration history.
Next.js App Router, TanStack Query, and Zustand on the frontend — server cache and UI state kept deliberately separate.
Redis doing three jobs at once: pub/sub for live tracking, caching, and BullMQ for background work.
detail.challenge: Making delivery tracking real-time without tying the WebSocket gateway to a single server. The Redis adapter for Socket.io solves this — any API instance can broadcast a tracking update and every connected client receives it, regardless of which instance they're attached to.
detail.status: Core product loop complete end-to-end and tested — 226 backend and 147 frontend tests, an 11-table data model, full seller/carrier self-signup with admin approval, shipment creation with real matching, and dashboards for all three roles. Operator invites and the notifications module (email/SLA alerts via BullMQ) are next on the roadmap.

vigilDashboard.description: A live global monitoring dashboard aggregating crypto markets, ISS tracking, seismic activity, weather and news into one real-time interface — React, a Three.js globe, WebSocket and REST polling side by side.

detail.overview: A live global monitoring dashboard aggregating eight independent data sources — crypto markets, ISS tracking, seismic activity, natural events, weather, and news — into one dense, responsive interface, built to demonstrate integrating heterogeneous real-time systems without the UI falling apart under the load.
architecture: Every widget shares one WidgetShell — header, LIVE indicator, loading/error/retry state — so visual consistency doesn't depend on repeating logic per widget.
Summary-page-plus-dedicated-pages pattern: the dashboard shows every widget in miniature, and each domain gets its own deeper page for detail and interactivity.
Heavy visualizations (the 3D globe, Leaflet maps) are isolated into their own lazy-loaded chunks — the initial dashboard load never waits on a ~470KB 3D vendor bundle.
stack: React 19 with Vite 8 (Rolldown) for fast builds and route-based code splitting via lazy() + Suspense.
TanStack Query for server cache and deduplication across eight independent APIs; Zustand for the genuinely global state — selected cryptos, the Binance WebSocket buffer, geolocation, alerts.
react-globe.gl, Recharts, and Leaflet, each scoped to the one domain that needs it, so no page pays for a visualization library it doesn't use.
detail.challenge: Keeping the dashboard fluid while eight sources with different transports — WebSocket, REST polling, RSS/XML, geolocation — update independently. The Binance WebSocket only connects on the /crypto page, not the dashboard, and every list component that receives frequent updates is memoized — together they keep the summary view light even with everything else running underneath.
detail.status: Feature-complete and deployed. All eight data domains have both a dashboard widget and a dedicated page.

realtimeCommunication.description: An interactive, side-by-side comparison of Polling, Long Polling, Server-Sent Events and WebSocket — live event streams for each technique, plus a bilingual technical deep-dive presentation.

detail.overview: An interactive, side-by-side comparison of the four real ways to get live data on the web — Polling, Long Polling, Server-Sent Events, and WebSocket — built from a technical talk delivered in Portuguese and rewritten here as a bilingual deep-dive with a working demo attached.
architecture: A single Express + ws backend runs all four techniques in parallel against the same simulated price feed, so the comparison is a live measurement, not a slide.
Each technique has its own connection hook on the frontend and its own request counter — the point is to make the cost of each approach visible in real time, not just describe it.
Below the md breakpoint the four panels become full-screen, swipeable slides instead of a cramped four-column grid.
stack: Plain Express + ws on the API — no framework overhead where the whole point is showing the raw mechanics of each transport.
Next.js App Router on the frontend, one hook per technique's connection logic, kept intentionally uncoupled from each other.
detail.challenge: Writing a production-grade SSE hook, not a toy one — exponential backoff, jitter to avoid a thundering herd on reconnect, stable callbacks via useLatestRef, and real cleanup on unmount. It's covered end-to-end, code and reasoning, in the deck's SSE module.
detail.status: Live demo and full bilingual slide deck (10 modules), both complete.

dineOutApp.description: A restaurant and bar discovery app — browse by cuisine, occasion and vibe, dig into a menu and reviews. Expo/React Native, built with a spec-driven workflow; currently a navigable prototype for business partners.

detail.overview: A restaurant and bar discovery app — browse by cuisine, occasion, and vibe, dig into a menu and reviews. Currently a navigable prototype for business partners: no backend yet, every screen reads from local mocks through a mocked network layer, so the seam to a real API is already in place rather than bolted on later.
architecture: A bulletproof-react-inspired structure adapted for React Native/Expo — each feature is an isolated vertical module (api/components/hooks/stores/types) that never imports another feature directly.
Every screen goes through TanStack Query hooks backed by MSW-mocked handlers, never a mock file directly — swapping in a real API later means changing the api/ layer, not the components.
Built spec-driven: every feature has a written spec (user stories, functional requirements, an architecture mapping) before any code, kept in sync with the implementation as it evolves.
stack: Expo (React Native + web from one codebase) with Expo Router for file-based navigation.
TanStack Query for server state, Zustand reserved for state genuinely needed by more than one feature.
MSW as the mocked network layer — tests and the running app hit the exact same handlers.
detail.challenge: Designing the mock-to-real-API seam correctly from day one, so a solo project without a backend yet doesn't end up needing a rewrite once one exists. Every component reads through a query hook, never a mock file — the day a real API shows up, only that hook's implementation changes.
detail.status: Navigable prototype, no backend. EAS Build is configured for internal APK distribution but hasn't been triggered yet.

portfolio.description: This very portfolio — built with Next.js, Three.js and Framer Motion.

detail.overview: This site. Four full-screen sections stacked with position: sticky and driven by a custom scroll-snap controller, with per-section entrance choreography, a Three.js particle field, and a scroll-linked exit parallax on the Hero section.
architecture: A single ScrollContainer owns scroll state and exposes it through React context, so any component — nav, section indicator, a section's own exit animation — can react to the current section without prop drilling.
next-intl with a locale segment ([locale]) for full EN/PT-BR content, not just UI strings.
A semantic color-token system in Tailwind v4's @theme block — named roles (highlight, body, muted-warm, dim) instead of one base color with an ad-hoc opacity ladder.
stack: Framer Motion for choreography, Three.js for the Hero's particle field.
Tailwind CSS v4 — CSS-based @theme configuration, no tailwind.config.js.
detail.challenge: Building a scroll-linked parallax for a position: sticky section. useScroll's target/offset mode measures the target's bounding rect — but a stuck sticky element's rect stops changing the moment it sticks, so the naive approach silently produces zero movement. The fix: read scrollTop/clientHeight directly from the scroll container instead of relying on element geometry.
detail.status: Actively evolving — most recently, dedicated case-study pages for each project, this one included.
